entry.title: Oxford study challenges the link between painkillers, the pill and blood clots

media:group.media:title: Oxford study challenges the link between painkillers, the pill and blood clots
media:group.media:description:
Oxford research challenges previous concerns about the risk of blood clots from taking common painkillers alongside hormonal contraception.
Analysing healthcare data from over 3 million women across four European countries, researchers found that blood clot risk was already elevated before women started taking painkillers like ibuprofen.
The findings suggest that underlying health conditions, rather than the medications alone, may help explain the increased risk.
NDORM's Prof Xintong Li explains what the team discovered.
Find out more about the research ⬇️ https://www.ndorms.ox.ac.uk/news/study-challenges-fears-over-blood-clot-risk-from-painkillers-and-hormonal-contraception

entry.title: You can recognise more faces than you think 👀

media:group.media:title: You can recognise more faces than you think 👀
media:group.media:description:
Research suggests we know around 5,000 faces on average 🤯
Isaac Winterburn, a DPhil student at the Oxford Department of Experimental Psychology, explains how our brains recognise thousands of faces, and why some people are particularly good at it.
References:
- Galdi, C., Nappi, M., Riccio, D., & Wechsler, H. (2016). Eye movement analysis for human authentication: a critical survey. Pattern Recognition Letters, 84, 272-283.
- Jenkins, R., Dowsett, A. J., & Burton, A. M. (2018). How many faces do people know?. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, 285(1888), 20181319. Robertson, D. J., Noyes, E., Dowsett, A. J., Jenkins, R., & Burton, A. M. (2016). Face recognition by metropolitan police super-recognisers. PloS one, 11(2), e0150036.
- Russell, R., Duchaine, B., & Nakayama, K. (2009). Super-recognizers: People with extraordinary face recognition ability. Psychonomic bulletin & review, 16(2), 252-257.
